For a molecule to be IR active (show an infrared spectrum), it needs to have a changing dipole moment during vibration. Let me analyze each molecule:

A. CO2 (Carbon dioxide): Linear molecule (O=C=O). While it has no permanent dipole moment due to its symmetry, its asymmetric stretching and bending vibrations create a changing dipole moment, making it IR active.

B. HCCH (Acetylene): Linear molecule (H-C≡C-H). It has symmetric and asymmetric stretching modes, with the asymmetric modes producing a changing dipole moment, making it IR active.

C. N2 (Nitrogen): Diatomic molecule (N≡N). It is completely symmetric and has only one vibrational mode (stretching). This stretching does not create a changing dipole moment because the electron distribution remains symmetric throughout the vibration. N2 is therefore IR inactive.

D. Benzene (C6H6): Planar, highly symmetric molecule. Despite its symmetry, it has several vibrational modes that create changing dipole moments, making it IR active.

Based on this analysis, the molecule that does not show an infrared spectrum is N2 (nitrogen).
